q: A page asks for 5 pieces of data one after another from a server across the world. Each trip takes 150 ms and each call does 1 ms of work. About how long does the page wait?
why: 5 x (150 + 1) = 755 ms. The trips add up. If the five calls do not need each other, ask them together and wait for the slowest only: about 151 ms.

q: Why does a brand new HTTPS connection to a far server cost about 3 round trips before the first byte?
options: One trip to open the line, one to agree the lock, one to ask and start the answer
The data is sent three times
Three servers each check the request
why: Open the line (TCP), agree the lock (TLS), then send the request. Keeping the connection open skips the first two.

q: Why do we round the seconds in a day to 100,000 when we estimate?
options: It makes the division easy, and the error is smaller than the error in the other guesses
why: A day is 86,400 seconds. The 16% error is small next to a guess like "1 million users". Round, say "about", and move on.

q: 2 million users a day each make 3 requests. About how many requests a second at the peak (3 times the average), and how many simple servers (1,000 a second each)?
why: 6,000,000 / 100,000 = 60 a second. Times 3 is 180. That is well under 1,000, so 1 server.

q: A design saves 5 KB per post and gets 4 million posts a day. About how much data is that in a year?
why: 4,000,000 x 5 KB = 20 GB a day. Times 365 is 7.3 TB a year. That is above 1 TB, so storage is the hard part.

q: A team sizes its servers for the average traffic only. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, the average is the right number
They fall over at the busy time, which can be 3 times the average or more
why: A system must survive the peak, not the average. Triple the average as a first guess, then replace it with the real shape when you know it.
